title: Millennium Ecosystem Assessment

definition.text: A major United Nations-backed study of how people affect the environment, called for in 2000, launched in 2001 and published in 2005.

facts.text: It popularized the term ecosystem services, meaning the benefits people gain from ecosystems.
More than 1300 authors from 95 countries contributed over four years.
It sorted ecosystem services into four groups: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting, with supporting services underpinning the other three.
It found that in the past 50 years humans changed ecosystems faster and more widely than ever before, mainly to meet demand for food, fresh water, timber, fibre and fuel.
These changes brought gains in well-being and development, but at the cost of degrading many ecosystem services and deepening poverty for some groups.
Its bottom line was that human actions are depleting Earth's natural capital so much that ecosystems' ability to sustain future generations can no longer be taken for granted.
Gretchen Daily's book Nature's Services was described as a catalyst for the assessment.
The 2019 IPBES global assessment was the first UN report on the state of biodiversity since the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005.

title: Ecological goods and services

definition.text: The economic benefits, in goods and services, that come from the natural workings of ecosystems.

facts.text: Ecological goods include clean air and plentiful fresh water; services include purifying air and water, breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, recharging groundwater and mitigating greenhouse gases.
They are a kind of public good.
They are being lost at an unsustainable rate, especially where land is converted from its natural state and loses its ecological functions.
A market can be created in which society demands these goods and services and public and private landowners supply them.
Paying farmers to set aside land marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'.
Biodiversity underlies them, supporting services such as biological control and genetic resources.
Gretchen Daily's original definition separated ecosystem goods from ecosystem services, but Costanza and colleagues and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment lumped both together as ecosystem services.
Besides paying landowners, their supply can be secured through regulation, stewardship programmes, eco-labelling, offset credits and tax rebates.

notes: Largely a synonym of Ecosystem service; the merge or selection pass may fold it in.

title: Nature's Services (1997)

definition.text: Gretchen Daily's edited book Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems, published in 1997, which laid out the framework widely used for understanding nature's benefits to people.

facts.text: It opens with Daily's introduction 'What are Ecosystem Services' and a history of the idea by Harold Mooney and Paul Ehrlich.
It and Costanza and colleagues' global valuation were the two seminal 1990s works on ecosystem services.
It served as a model for ecosystem regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

title: History of the ecosystem services idea

definition.text: How the idea that ecosystems provide services to people grew from ancient observations into a standard scientific term.

facts.text: Around 400 BC Plato understood that cutting down forests could cause soil erosion and dry up springs.
Modern ideas probably began in 1864, when Marsh challenged the belief that Earth's resources are unlimited by pointing to changing soil fertility around the Mediterranean.

In the late 1940s Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr, William Vogt and Aldo Leopold promoted the idea that people depend on the environment; in 1956 Paul Sears stressed ecosystems' role in processing wastes and recycling nutrients.
In 1970 Paul Ehrlich and Rosa Weigert warned that human activity could destroy the ecological systems on which the human species depends.
The term 'environmental services' appeared in a 1970 report listing insect pollination, fisheries, climate regulation and flood control; 'ecosystem services' later became the standard term.
E. F. Schumacher coined the term 'natural capital' in his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful.
In the 1990s Gretchen Daily's Nature's Services and Costanza and colleagues' first attempt to put a money value on ecosystem services became the two seminal works.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularised the idea in the early 2000s, and it has kept expanding to include social, economic and conservation goals.

definition.text: The effort to express what ecosystem services are worth in economic terms, so that their value can be weighed in decisions.

facts.text: Many efforts translate scientific knowledge into economics, stating the results of choices in comparable units of impact on human well-being.
The idea is that, although people decide for many reasons, overall trends reveal a society's preferences, from which a service's value can be inferred.
A hard problem is that ecological information gathered at one scale of space and time may not apply at another.
The six main ways of valuing services in money are avoided cost, replacement cost, factor income, travel cost, hedonic pricing and contingent valuation.
Factor income counts how a service raises incomes, as when cleaner water increases a fishery's catch and fishers' earnings.
Salles (2011) argued that the total value of biodiversity is infinite, so debating nature's total worth is pointless because we cannot live without it.
As of 2012 many companies did not fully grasp how much they depend on ecosystems; most corporate environmental tools track impacts rather than dependence.
Tools that help businesses value services include the 2008 Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, the ARIES project from 2007 and InVEST from 2012.

title: Ecosystem service trade-offs

definition.text: Cases where using or boosting one ecosystem service reduces others or harms some people, as opposed to synergies, where services rise together.

facts.text: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found many ways to conserve or enhance particular services that reduce negative trade-offs or create positive synergies with other services.
Nutrient cycling cannot simply be dialled to the best level: heavy fertilizer use in the US Midwest has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico.
In some areas there is a trade-off between farm production and restoring ecosystems.
Decisions about ecosystems create winners and losers, such as water moved from poor to rich users or a protected wetland that limits fishing rights.
Valuation can give extra weight to a service's irreplaceability or to bundled services that come together.
Tools such as InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs) and the Freshwater Health Index help managers assess trade-offs.
Landscape planning tries to exploit synergies and manage trade-offs among food production, conservation and livelihoods.

notes: No page or section of its own; passes the curriculum test by mentions on Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, Ecosystem ecology, Climate change adaptation, Agroecosystem, Ecosystem service, Conservation International and Agricultural biodiversity.

title: Beneficiaries of ecosystem services

definition.text: The people who gain from a given ecosystem service, whether they live beside the ecosystem or feel its effects only indirectly.

facts.text: Some services, such as fresh water, food or beauty, directly affect nearby people's livelihoods, while others, such as climate or erosion regulation, affect people indirectly.
Ecological goods and services benefit all living things, including animals and plants, not humans alone.
In private payment deals, beneficiaries are expected to pay a price lower than the welfare gain they get from the service.
Paying landowners who supply services marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'.

notes: No page of its own; mentioned on Ecosystem service, Ecological goods and services and Payment for ecosystem services.

definition.text: Efforts to protect ecosystem services through policy, institutions and management, which face large practical hurdles even where services have money values.

facts.text: Decision-makers must balance present and future human needs, often working from valid but incomplete information.
Existing laws are often seen as inadequate because they rest on human-health standards that do not match what protecting ecosystem health requires.
As of 2005, local to regional collective management was considered suitable for services such as crop pollination and for resources like water.
Since the 1990s, marketing ecosystem service protection has grown, with credits for activities such as protecting carbon sinks or restoring service providers.
Such schemes need clearly defined land rights, often missing in developing countries, and raise worries about inconsistent compensation.
Because protecting services often overlaps with protecting biodiversity, merging the two goals has been suggested.
As of 2018 the concept was not yet properly built into international and regional law, though Sustainable Development Goal 15 targets conserving, restoring and sustainably using ecosystem services.
Ecosystem services are estimated to add $125 trillion to $140 trillion to the economy each year; climate-driven biome shifts may cut them by 9% globally by 2100.

definition.text: Making land-use choices that affect ecosystem services, which means weighing ecology, technology, society and the economy together.

facts.text: These decisions are usually spatial, always have several objectives, and rest on uncertain data, models and estimates.
They must weigh all stakeholders' views, from regulators and developers to residents and NGOs; usually the best science combined with stakeholder values drives the process.
Studies have modelled stakeholders as agents, used Monte Carlo methods to capture uncertainty in landowner choices, and used Bayesian networks to combine uncertain science with stakeholder input.
Remote sensing can track the health and extent of land cover that provides services, helping planning, monitoring and communication between stakeholders.

definition.text: Using life-cycle assessment, which tracks the environmental pressures of making products, to estimate how human activities change ecosystem services.

facts.text: Life-cycle assessment impact methods link pressures such as land-use change and eutrophication to changes in ecological functions and ecosystem services.
A 2026 review found three main kinds of model: land-use impact models, extended ecosystem quality models and inventory-based models.
The models differ in which services and ecosystems they cover, their indicators, and whether they count service supply, demand or both, which limits comparison.
Freshwater and marine services remain poorly represented, so more consistent methodological guidance is needed.

title: Nature's contributions to people
article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Nature's contributions to people

definition.text: The IPBES term for all the ways nature benefits people, adopted in place of 'nature's benefits to people'.

facts.text: The 5th IPBES Plenary in 2017 decided to use the concept in current and future assessments.
It was introduced to bring diverse worldviews, including indigenous and local knowledge, into biodiversity assessments.
Some scientists objected that the term was confusing and not significantly different from ecosystem services.

contested_note: Scientists disagree whether the term adds anything beyond the ecosystem services concept.
